question: A 39-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, at 32 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and nausea. She has had one episode of nonbloody vomiting. Pregnancy has been uncomplicated, except for a blood pressure measurement of 150/90 mm Hg on her last prenatal visit. Her first child was delivered vaginally; her second child was delivered by lower segment transverse cesarean section because of a nonreassuring fetal heart rate. She appears anxious and pale. Her temperature is 36.1°C (96°F), pulse is 115/min, and blood pressure is 92/65 mm Hg. Extremities are cool and clammy. Pelvic examination shows a rigid, tender uterus. The cervix is 30% effaced and 1 cm dilated; the vertex is at -1 station. The fetal heart rate is 100/min. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Abruptio placentae -> sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and nausea -> 80% CHAIN: Abruptio placentae -> rigid, tender uterus on pelvic examination -> 75% CHAIN: Abruptio placentae -> nonreassuring fetal heart rate -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis in this case is abruptio placentae. The sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and nausea, along with a rigid, tender uterus on pelvic examination and a nonreassuring fetal heart rate, are highly indicative of abruptio placentae. The evidence paths linking abruptio placentae to symptoms like nausea, infection, and anemia further support this diagnosis.
analysis: The core medical principle in this case is the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain and nausea in a pregnant woman with a rigid, tender uterus and nonreassuring fetal heart rate, which strongly suggests abruptio placentae. The enhanced information provided aligns with the classic presentation of abruptio placentae, further supporting this diagnosis.
